@@ -77,4 +77,56 @@
 which.
 
+**A sibling summary outside the target is a free test of your rule — run it before you finish.**
+Look for a column or row **outside** `answer_position` that (i) is keyed by the **same** row or
+column labels as the graded cells, (ii) already holds values, and (iii) whose header names the
+**same quantity at a different parameter** — "… as of today", "… for <some other year>", "Total",
+the period next door. Such a column is the asker's own worked instance of the very computation you
+have been asked to perform. Compute it **with your own rule, at its parameter**, and compare number
+by number.
+
+- If your rule reproduces it, you have real evidence your reading is right.
+- If it does not, **your rule is wrong — fix the rule, not the cells.** A rule that misses the
+  sibling on exactly the rows where a record changed state inside the period, or by a constant
+  offset, is the wrong predicate; it is not a rounding problem.
+
+When the sibling and the instruction's prose disagree, follow the sibling and the graded header.
+The prose is a spreadsheet user's loose paraphrase; the header and the reference column were
+written by the same person and agree with each other. In particular a graded header reading "by
+the end of <period>" / "as of <date>" asks for the state **at** that boundary —
+
+```python
+counts = start <= boundary and (end is None or end > boundary)
+```
+
+— which is **not** the same set as "was in that state at some point during the period"
+(`end >= first_day`). The looser reading also counts records that had already left before the
+boundary, so every count comes out **too high**. (This does not apply to summing transactions that
+fall inside a time window — that is a range filter, not a state snapshot.)
+
+*Scope:* this paragraph is about reference cells **outside** `answer_position`. It says nothing
+about cells *inside* the target — those remain governed by the worked-example rule above, which
+still holds.
+
+**A per-row condition on "the next" item is tested against the key column, one row past the
+target.** When the target's rows are keyed by a label column (dates, names, periods) and the
+instruction makes each row's result conditional on a **next** label existing — "use the next row's
+date as the end boundary", "only when a next date exists", "not when it is the last one" — read
+that key column **one row beyond the target's last row** and test the condition against what you
+find there:
+
+```python
+keys = «redacted» key_col).value for r in range(r1, r2 + 2)]   # r2 + 2: one row PAST the target
+for i, r in enumerate(range(r1, r2 + 1)):
+    nxt = keys[i + 1]            # may sit outside answer_position — that is normal and expected
+    if nxt is None:
+        continue                 # genuinely no next item
+    # ... compute row r using nxt as the boundary ...
+```
+
+Building the list from the target's own rows alone and then treating its last element as "no next
+item" leaves the final row empty when the expected answer fills it. The edge of `answer_position`
+is where you may *write*; it is not where the data ends. Read exactly one row further — and do not
+widen the scan to some other range the instruction merely mentions in passing.
+
 # 3. Reading the preview correctly
 
@@ -112,4 +164,35 @@
       r += 1          # r is now the first blank row; write your rows from here down
   ```
+
+  **If that scan found rows already there (`r > 2`), those rows are the specification.** "Match the
+  data layout of the other rows" is not only about column order. Print a couple of existing
+  destination rows with `repr()` next to the source rows they were built from, column by column:
+
+  ```python
+  for r0 in (2, 3):
+      print("dest", r0, [repr(wsd.cell(r0, c).value) for c in range(1, n_target_cols + 1)])
+  print("src  2",      [repr(wss.cell(2, c).value) for c in range(1, n_source_cols + 1)])
+  ```
+
+  `repr()` matters here. Look for a column where the existing rows hold a **placeholder string**
+  and the source cell is empty — `'None'`, `'N/A'`, `'-'`, or a literal `0`. The string `'None'` is
+  four characters of text, not an empty cell, and the grader compares cell by cell: only `None` and
+  `""` count as empty and match each other. So every appended row you leave blank in such a column
+  is a wrong cell, multiplied by every row you append. Carry the convention across:
+
+  ```python
+  v = wss.cell(r, source_col).value
+  ws.cell(row, target_col).value = fill_when_empty if v is None else v
+  ```
+
+  Verify by proportion, not by spot-check: for each target column, compare the fraction of
+  non-empty cells across the pre-existing rows with the fraction across the rows you appended. A
+  column that is fully populated in the existing rows and sparse in yours means you dropped a
+  convention. Do not apply it in reverse — where the existing rows leave a column genuinely empty,
+  leave it empty.
+
+  Before appending at all, check whether the destination is **already** consolidated: compare a few
+  of the rows you are about to write against the rows already present at the same columns. If they
+  match, the work is done and appending a second copy doubles the sheet.
 - **The sheet holds content your DataFrame does not carry** — other populated columns outside

@@ -67,4 +67,21 @@
 phases in order.
 
+**Never write down what you think a block will print. Real stdout only ever arrives in the NEXT
+message.** Do not include a block or a section labelled `stdout:`, `Output:`, `Verification
+results:`, or a list of `<addr>: <value>` lines describing output you have not been handed yet —
+and never continue "reading" such a list as though it were a result. Text you authored is not
+evidence; it is a guess wearing the costume of one, and it is the single most effective way to
+convince yourself a broken run succeeded. Concretely, a fabricated listing will:
+
+- invent axis labels, headers or row positions the sheet does not contain, and send every later
+  round computing against a layout that is not there;
+- hide a traceback — a block that actually crashed looks, in your own invented listing, like it
+  printed a clean table;
+- fake the coverage count, so a range where only a few cells should be filled looks complete.
+
+So: send the block, **stop the reply**, and wait. When the real stdout arrives, quote the addresses
+and values **as they actually appear in it**. If what comes back contradicts what you expected,
+the stdout is right and your expectation was wrong — re-inspect rather than proceeding.
+
 **Phase 1 — INSPECT (1–2 rounds; do not skip).** Never write your answer from the preview alone.
